Lancaster's population increased by around 4,600 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population passed 140,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Lancaster increased by 3.3%, from just under 138,400 in 2011 to around 142,900 in 2021.

The population here increased by a smaller percentage than the overall population of the North West (5.2%), and by a smaller percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Lancaster was home to around 1.8 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 1.7 in 2011. This area was among the lowest 30% for population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was lower in Lancaster than across the North West

Median age stable in Lancaster

The latest census data also show that the average (median) age remained 40 years in Lancaster between the last two censuses.

This area had a similar average (median) age to the North West as a whole in 2021 (40 years) and had a similar averaage (median) age to England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 50 to 64 years rose by just over 2,800 (an increase of 11.3%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by around 2,500 (9.5% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 50 and 64 years increased by 1.4 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Disability in Lancaster

Lancaster saw the North West's largest percentage-point rise in the proportion of residents who were identified as disabled and limited a little (from 10.7% in 2011 to 11.7% in 2021). These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

Wirral saw the North West's next largest increase in the proportion of residents who were identified as disabled and limited a little (from 10.7% in 2011 to 11.6% in 2021).

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a little in Lancaster increased by 1.0 percentage points

Health in Lancaster

In 2021, 46.4% of Lancaster residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 45.3% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" rose from 34.3% to 34.4%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Lancaster residents describing their health as "very bad" was 1.3% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 4.7% to 4.4%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very good health in Lancaster increased by 1.1 percentage points

Unpaid care in Lancaster

In 2021, 4.8% of Lancaster residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 7.3% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The decrease in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Lancaster (2.5 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the North West (2.7 percentage points, from 7.2% to 4.5%). Across England, the proportion fell by 2.8 percentage points, from 7.2% to 4.4%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Lancaster decreased by 2.5 percentage points

Religion in Lancaster

In 2021, 38.1% of Lancaster residents reported having "No religion", up from 24.5% in 2011. The rise of 13.6 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Lancaster. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the North West, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 19.8% to 32.6%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 51.8% of people in Lancaster described themselves as Christian (down from 65.9%), while 6.6% did not state their religion (down from 7.1% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

Lancaster residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 124,300 Lancaster residents said they were born in England. This represented 86.9% of the local population. The figure has risen from around 122,700 in 2011, which at the time represented 88.7% of Lancaster's population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with around 2,800 Lancaster residents reporting this country of birth (2.0%). This figure was down from around 3,300 in 2011, which at the time represented 2.3% of the population of Lancaster.

The number of Lancaster residents born in Poland rose from just under 1,800 in 2011 (1.3% of the local population) to around 2,400 in 2021 (1.7%).

In 2021, 86.9% of Lancaster residents reported their country of birth as England

National identity in Lancaster

In 2021, 6.8% of Lancaster residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 5.1% in 2011.

In 2021, 1.6% of residents identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 0.6% in 2011. The percentage of residents in Lancaster that identified as "British only" increased from 16.8% to 56.3%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater across the North West (2.3 percentage points, from 4.7% to 7.1%) than in Lancaster (1.6 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Lancaster increased by 1.6 percentage points

Family in Lancaster

Of Lancaster households, 17.8% included a couple but no children in 2021, down from 18.6% in 2011.

The decrease in the percentage of households including a couple but no children was greater in Lancaster (0.8 percentage points) than across the North West (0.5 percentage points, from 16.5% to 16.0%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.9 percentage points, from 17.6% to 16.8%.

The percentage of households including a couple without children in Lancaster decreased by 0.8 percentage points

More adults never married or in a civil partnership

Of Lancaster residents aged 16 years and over, 40.4% said they had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2021, up from 37.3% in 2011.

In 2021, just over 4 in 10 people (41.4%) said they were married or in a registered civil partnership, compared with 43.5% in 2011. The percentage of adults in Lancaster that had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership remained at 9.5%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership was greater across the North West (3.8 percentage points, from 35.6% to 39.4%) than in Lancaster (3.1 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.3 percentage points, from 34.6% to 37.9%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in Lancaster increased by 3.1 percentage points

Change in employment

Of Lancaster residents aged 16 years and over, 49.7% said they were employed (excluding full-time students) in 2021, down from 51.0% in 2011.

In 2021, around 1 in 50 people (2.0%) said they were unemployed, compared with 2.9% in 2011. The percentage of retired Lancaster residents increased from 23.4% to 23.9%.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed was greater in Lancaster (1.3 percentage points) than across the North West (0.5 percentage points, from 54.2% to 53.7%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.8 percentage points, from 56.5% to 55.7%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in Lancaster decreased by 1.3 percentage points

Working hours in Lancaster

In 2021, 12.2% of Lancaster residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked 15 hours or less per week. This figure was at a similar level in 2011 (12.1%).

In 2021, just under one in nine people (10.6%) said they worked over 49 hours per week, compared with 12.4% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 53.5% to 55.2%.

This area had the region’s third highest percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week. Across the region, only South Lakeland (13.2%) and Eden (12.5%) had a higher percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in Lancaster increased by 0.1 percentage points

Change in housing in Lancaster

Of Lancaster households, 67.1% owned their home in 2021, down from 69.2% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in five households (21.7%) rented privately, compared with 18.9% in 2011. The percentage of Lancaster households that lived in a socially rented property increased from 10.0% to 10.3%.

The decrease in the percentage of households that owned their home in Lancaster (2.0 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the North West (2.2 percentage points, from 64.5% to 62.3%). Across England, the percentage fell by 2.0 percentage points, from 63.3% to 61.3%.

The rate of home ownership in Lancaster decreased by 2.0 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Lancaster

In 2021, 3.6% of Lancaster residents identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category, up from 2.7% in 2011. The 0.9 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the North West, the percentage of people from the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" ethnic group increased from 6.2% to 8.4%, while across England the percentage increased from 7.8% to 9.6%.

In 2021, 93.1% of people in Lancaster identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 95.6% in 2011), while 1.5% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 1.0% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.2% in 2011 to 0.9% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
